newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungary crossroads of organised crime, police say.
newsitem.headline: Hungary crossroads of organised crime, police say.

text.p: Hungary has become a European crossroads for organised crime and the international police response to combat the upsurge has been inadequate, a top Hungarian crimefighter said on Tuesday.

"Hungary has become the crossroads of eastern and western (European) criminals," Laszlo Tonnhauser, head of the Hungarian police's organised crime unit told a three-day conference attended by police chiefs from 14 countries.
"Inefficient states and international relations hinder our job," he said.

The conference, attended by high-ranking police officers from Europe, the United States, South Africa, Israel, Interpol and Europol, focused on the spread of organised crime from the former Soviet Union through Europe.
The Russian delegation cancelled its appearance at the last minute.
Tonnhauser said that although organised crime first appeared in Hungary in the late 1970s, the presence of international criminals is a relatively new phenomenon.
"Ethnic criminal groups appeared in Hungary after the mass privatisation started in 1989-90," Tonnhauser said.
Apart from the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS), organised crime was also inported into Hungary from South America, Turkey, Italy, Nigeria and Kosovo, in Serbia, he said.
Hungary's Minister of the Interior Gabor Kuncze said the spread of criminals from the former Soviet Union had caught Europe unguarded.
"An east-west movement from the CIS caused many problems...and the international response was lacking in efficiency," Kuncze said.
He added that Hungary, earlier a transit station for drugs trafficking, car theft and arms smuggling was increasingly becoming a drugs consumer itself.
"In 1990, police seized six kilograms of drugs -- in 1996 the amount was almost one tonne," Kuncze said.
Tonnhauser added that modern organised crime present in Hungary is "technically proficient and incredibly brutal".
He also said that police can only crack the relatively simple cases while most of the major ones remain unpunished both in Hungary and other countries.
Tonnhauser said concerted international action against organised crime should be a top priority as it threatens not only individuals but the fabric of societies.
"Organised crime is a threat against democracy," Tonnhauser said.
